37.q: What is a game, at its most basic level?
opts: A set of interacting systems and rules
37.why: A game is systems: rules that take input and produce output. Story and levels are content built on top of those systems.
37.wrongWhy: The other answers are things a game can contain, but none of them is what makes it a game. A story without interacting systems is a film.

37.q: What is a 'system' in game design?
opts: Anything that takes an input, applies a rule, and produces an output
37.why: A system is an input, a rule, and an output. Jump, enemy contact, and economy are all systems.
37.wrongWhy: An engine runs the game but is not itself a design system, and a level is content, not a rule.

37.q: Why design systems instead of scenes?
opts: A system is a rule you can tune with one number; a scene is fixed content
Scenes are more fun to build
37.why: Tuning one number in a system changes the whole game. Changing a scene only changes that scene.
37.wrongWhy: The other answers describe preferences or performance, not the design advantage of rules over fixed content.

37.q: What is the core loop?
opts: The longest level in the game
The shortest cycle of actions the player repeats
37.why: The core loop is the repeated cycle: move, fight, collect, upgrade, repeat. Everything else feeds it or interrupts it.
37.wrongWhy: The other answers are single moments or screens, not the repeating cycle the player spends most of their time in.

37.q: A good core loop has three parts. What are they?
37.why: Goal, obstacle, reward. Kill the enemy (goal), it shoots back (obstacle), it drops coins (reward).
37.wrongWhy: The other lists describe structure or screens, not the three functional parts of a repeating loop.

37.q: What is the most common core-loop mistake?
opts: A loop that is fun for thirty seconds and then repeats identically forever
37.why: A loop with no change goes flat. The fix is not more content but making the reward change the next loop.
37.wrongWhy: The other options are not the core problem: length, reward count, and clarity are separate issues.

37.q: What makes a reward actually a reward?
opts: It changes what the player does next
37.why: If the reward does not change the next loop, it is just a score. A real reward alters the player's options.
37.wrongWhy: The other answers are presentation or rarity, which do not change the player's behaviour.

37.q: What is 'juice' in games?
opts: The extra layer of feedback on top of the mechanics
37.why: Juice is feedback: screen shake, hitstop, particles, sound, anticipation. It changes how the game feels without changing the rules.
37.wrongWhy: The other answers are content or performance, not the feedback layer that makes events feel impactful.

37.q: Which of these gives the most game feel for the least effort?
37.why: Screen shake has the highest impact-to-effort ratio in games. A tiny camera offset on impact reads as weight.
37.wrongWhy: The other options are expensive visual work that changes little about how the game feels to play.

37.q: What is 'anticipation' in animation?
opts: Making the character crouch for a few frames before jumping
Playing a sound before an event
37.why: Anticipation is a small preparatory motion before the main action. The player's eye follows the intent, not the movement.
37.wrongWhy: The other answers are longer or unrelated; anticipation is a few frames, not a whole animation or scene.

37.q: What should you NOT do with juice?
37.why: Juice marks what matters. If a pickup and a boss death get the same reaction, the player learns nothing is special.
37.wrongWhy: Adding juice to important events, scaling by impact, and testing in isolation are all correct practice.

37.q: What are the two engines that keep players playing?
37.why: Mastery: I am getting better and can feel it. Curiosity: I want to know what happens next.
37.wrongWhy: The other answers are features or content. Only mastery and curiosity are the psychological drivers.

37.q: What does 'mastery' need to work?
opts: Clear goals, immediate feedback, and difficulty that rises with skill
37.why: Mastery is served by clear goals, immediate feedback, and a rising challenge. Without those the player cannot feel improvement.
37.wrongWhy: The other answers are optional content. A scoreboard or a long story does not create the feeling of getting better.

37.q: What does 'curiosity' need?
opts: Information revealed slowly, with questions left unanswered
37.why: Curiosity comes from unanswered questions. Revealing everything immediately removes it.
37.wrongWhy: The other answers are content or polish; only slow revelation and unanswered questions create curiosity.

37.q: Why do close losses keep players playing?
opts: They feel like 'almost', so a different choice would have worked
37.why: A 9-10 loss feels like 'almost'. A 0-10 loss feels hopeless. Close losses invite another attempt.
37.wrongWhy: The other answers do not address the psychology: the feeling of near-success is what drives the retry.

37.q: What is the real difficulty dial in most platformers?
37.why: How far back the player restarts is what makes a platformer feel hard or fair. It costs progress, not dignity.
37.wrongWhy: The other options change challenge but not the felt difficulty as directly as how far back you restart.

37.q: What is the best order of difficulty dials by usefulness?
opts: Enemy speed, health and damage, reaction windows, resources, checkpoints
37.why: Enemy speed is the biggest dial because it changes how much time the player has to react, which changes everything.
37.wrongWhy: The other orders put the smaller dials first. Speed dominates because it affects every encounter.

37.q: Why is a 'ramp' of difficulty worse than a 'staircase'?
opts: A ramp has no landings, so the player never gets to consolidate a new skill
A ramp is more boring to draw
37.why: Staircase means rise, then land. The landing is where the player masters the new thing before the next challenge.
37.wrongWhy: The other answers are not about learning: a ramp fails because it denies the player consolidation time.

37.q: What is the 'landing' in a difficulty staircase?
opts: A place where the player practises the new skill without being punished for it
37.why: The landing is deliberate practice time. Without it the player is always slightly behind the difficulty.
37.wrongWhy: A safe room or checkpoint is a physical place; the landing is a design beat in the difficulty curve.

37.q: What is the three-beat pattern for teaching a mechanic?
37.why: Safe introduction (nothing can go wrong), test (they must use it to proceed), twist (it combines with something known).
37.wrongWhy: The other patterns miss the essential middle beat: the test that forces the player to actually use the mechanic.

37.q: Why do good games avoid text tutorials?
opts: A level that teaches is more effective than one that explains
37.why: Designing rooms, not tutorials. The player learns by doing, and the geometry carries the lesson.
37.wrongWhy: The other answers are practical concerns. The real reason is that learning by doing is more effective.

37.q: What is 'affordance'?
opts: What an object visually invites the player to do
37.why: A red barrel invites being shot. A ledge invites jumping. The object's look should tell the player what to do with it.
37.wrongWhy: The other answers are unrelated; affordance is about visual invitation, not cost, skill, or speed.

37.q: What is 'readability' in level design?
opts: How fast the player reads text
Whether the player can see the important thing at a glance
The font size of the UI
How many colours the level uses
37.why: Readability means the player can identify the next action instantly. Contrast and clear silhouettes create it.
37.wrongWhy: The other answers are about text or colour count, not about whether the important thing is visible.

37.q: The classic beginner level problem is:
37.why: Players do not fail from lack of skill — they fail because the game hid the information they needed.
37.wrongWhy: The other options are not the classic failure. Density and length are separate issues from readability.

37.q: What must the first 60 seconds contain?
opts: A clear goal, one success, and one moment of curiosity
37.why: Players decide in the first minute whether they stay. Goal, success, curiosity is the reliable recipe.
37.wrongWhy: The other answers are slow or demanding openings. A cutscene or boss fight delays the player's first success.

37.q: What is the most common opening mistake?
opts: A slow opening — walking, reading, watching — before the game starts
37.why: By the time the game starts, the player has already left. Cut the opening; you can always add it back.
37.wrongWhy: The other answers are not opening-specific failures. Speed, enemies, and music are separate concerns.

37.q: Why do games have quiet rooms between fights?
opts: They are the release that makes the tension meaningful
37.why: Tension needs release. Without the quiet, the fight stops feeling intense and the player goes numb.
37.wrongWhy: The other answers misunderstand pacing. The release is a design tool, not a cost saving or a rest area.

37.q: If every section of a game is equally intense, what happens?
37.why: Equal intensity everywhere is the same as no intensity anywhere. Contrast is what creates the feeling.
37.wrongWhy: The other answers are not consequences of flat intensity. The loss of contrast is the direct result.

37.q: What is the rule about player actions and reactions?
opts: Every action must have a visible reaction, even a failed one
37.why: If the player cannot tell 'it worked' from 'it did nothing', the game has lied to them.
37.wrongWhy: The other answers allow silent failures, which is exactly the problem the rule prevents.

37.q: What are the three rules of a good death?
opts: Readable, caused by the player's choice, fast to restart
37.why: The player should see what killed them, understand it was their decision, and restart quickly.
37.wrongWhy: The other answers either hide the cause or make the player wait, both of which feel unfair.

37.q: What is 'i-frames'?
opts: Invincibility frames after taking damage, preventing one swing draining a full health bar
37.why: Without i-frames a single enemy attack can hit multiple times in one swing and drain the whole bar.
37.wrongWhy: The other answers are unrelated systems. I-frames exist specifically to prevent multi-hit damage.

37.q: Why should the hurtbox be slightly smaller than the sprite?
opts: It makes the game feel forgiving when the player visually missed
37.why: If the art says 'I clearly missed' but the box says 'hit', the player blames the game. A smaller box avoids that.
37.wrongWhy: The other answers are not the reason. The forgiveness is a feel decision, not a performance or size one.

37.q: What makes a telegraphed attack fair?
opts: The player can see it coming and respond
37.why: A telegraphed attack gives the player information. Fairness comes from information, not from weakness.
37.wrongWhy: The other answers change the numbers but not the fairness. An untelegraphed fast attack is still unfair.

37.q: What is the cheapest way to make an enemy more interesting?
opts: Give it three states: idle, telegraph, attack
37.why: Three states with visible telegraphs create depth. Combinations of simple enemies beat new art.
37.wrongWhy: The other answers are numbers or art. States add behaviour, which is what the player actually reads.

37.q: What is depth in game design, according to this course?
opts: Combinations of simple systems creating new encounters without new assets
37.why: A fast enemy plus a ranged enemy in the same room is a new encounter without a new asset.
37.wrongWhy: The other answers add content or complexity. Depth is about combinations, not volume.

37.q: What is progression's job?
opts: To answer 'why am I still playing?' with something visible and slightly ahead
37.why: Progression must be visible, regular, and slightly ahead. Players quit in the gaps, not at the hard parts.
37.wrongWhy: The other answers are not the function of progression. Length and display are side effects, not the purpose.

37.q: What rhythm of rewards works best?
opts: One large reward at the end
Small rewards every few minutes, a medium one per level, a large one at the end
37.why: The small-medium-large rhythm keeps the player moving. A long gap with nothing is where players quit.
37.wrongWhy: The other answers either create a long empty gap or remove the sense of accumulating progress.

37.q: What makes a currency into a real economy?
opts: At least two competing uses for the same resource
37.why: With one use there is no economy, only a queue. Two competing uses force a real choice.
37.wrongWhy: The other answers are presentation or volume. Without a trade-off there is no decision to make.

37.q: What should an upgrade ideally change?
37.why: A jump that goes further changes your routes. A bigger number changes nothing about how the game plays.
37.wrongWhy: The other answers are cosmetic or numeric. The best upgrades change decisions, not values.

37.q: Why use a state machine?
opts: It replaces a tangle of if-statements with a list of states and the rules between them
It is required by the engine
37.why: A state machine lets you see every state and every transition in one place. Bugs live in the transitions you forgot.
37.wrongWhy: The other answers are not the benefit. The value is visibility of states and transitions.

37.q: Where do most state-machine bugs come from?
opts: A state that cannot be exited, or a transition that was never defined
37.why: If you can get into a state you must be able to get out. Missing transitions cause soft-locks.
37.wrongWhy: The other answers are not the source. The bug is almost always a missing rule, not broken logic.

37.q: What is the same pattern as a state machine, one level up?
opts: Game flow: menu, playing, paused, game over, victory
37.why: The game itself has states with entry and exit rules. The pause screen must actually pause; game over must offer a way back.
37.wrongWhy: The other answers are subsystems. Game flow is the top-level state machine of the whole game.

37.q: What is a boss fight's design brief?
opts: A wall to block the player
A test of everything the player has learned, using familiar mechanics under new pressure
37.why: A boss that teaches is a tutorial; a boss that surprises is a wall. Familiar mechanics under new pressure is the sweet spot.
37.wrongWhy: The other answers make the boss arbitrary. The brief is to test, not to block or show off.

37.q: Why do bosses have phases?
opts: Phases give the player clear progress and let the fight escalate without becoming unfair
37.why: Phases solve pacing in a long fight: visible progress plus escalation, with a natural breather between phases.
37.wrongWhy: The other answers are not the reason. Phases are a pacing and fairness tool.

37.q: What should the final blow of a boss do?
opts: Feel different — slow it down and give the player a moment of safety
37.why: The player should be able to tell they won without reading the health bar. A boss that dies like a normal enemy wastes the fight.
37.wrongWhy: The other answers miss the point. The final blow is about payoff, not numbers.

37.q: What is a state machine's minimum useful version?
opts: An enum of states and a match statement in the update function
37.why: An enum plus one match block is the whole pattern. Everything else is optional structure.
37.wrongWhy: The other answers add machinery you do not need. The enum and the match are sufficient.

37.q: What is the 'twist' beat in teaching a mechanic?
opts: The mechanic combining with something the player already knows
A harder version of the test
37.why: The twist integrates the new skill with an existing one, so the player remembers it instead of forgetting it in isolation.
37.wrongWhy: The other answers are not the twist. The twist is about combination, not difficulty or reward.

37.q: What is the most common reason players quit a beginner game?
opts: They do not know what to do next
37.why: Fix clarity before you fix balance. A confused player quits even when the difficulty is fair.
37.wrongWhy: The other answers are real problems but not the most common. Confusion is the primary cause.

37.q: What should you do first when a section feels too hard?
opts: Add information — a telegraph, a clearer path — before changing the numbers
37.why: If the player dies and says 'that was cheap', the fault is almost always missing information. Add information before adding difficulty.
37.wrongWhy: The other answers change numbers or length. The problem is usually unreadability, not difficulty.

37.q: What is the single highest-leverage design habit mentioned in this course?
opts: Expressing features as data instead of code
37.why: If content is a spreadsheet row rather than a new function, you can add a hundred items cheaply.
37.wrongWhy: The other answers do not scale. Data-driven content is the habit that lets a small developer do a large amount.

44.q: What does platformer movement feel depend on most?
opts: Three numbers: acceleration, stop speed, and jump height
44.why: Players feel acceleration, stop speed, and jump height. Gravity and jump height are tuned as a ratio, not independently.
44.wrongWhy: The other answers are not what the player feels. Realistic physics often feels worse in a platformer.

44.q: What asymmetry makes a jump feel weighty?
44.why: Rising gently and dropping decisively reads as weight. The asymmetry is what the player feels.
44.wrongWhy: The other answers remove the asymmetry. Equal rise and fall reads as floaty and weightless.

44.q: What is coyote time?
opts: Letting the player jump for about 0.1 seconds after walking off a ledge
44.why: Without coyote time, a jump pressed a frame too late fails and feels like the game ate the input.
44.wrongWhy: The other answers are unrelated. Coyote time is a small grace window after leaving a platform.

44.q: What is jump buffering?
opts: Remembering a jump pressed slightly before landing and firing it on landing
44.why: Without buffering, a well-timed jump on a moving platform fails silently and feels broken.
44.wrongWhy: The other answers change jump power. Buffering is about remembering the input, not about strength.

44.q: Why do players not notice coyote time and buffering when they work?
opts: They are only noticed when they are missing
They are too small to see
44.why: Players do not notice when they are there; they absolutely notice when they are not.
44.wrongWhy: The other answers are wrong. These features are invisible but their absence is glaring.

44.q: What does variable jump height do?
opts: Lets a tap give a small hop and a hold give a full jump
44.why: The button hold time controls the height. This single change makes platforming dramatically more controllable.
44.wrongWhy: The other answers add new abilities. Variable height uses the existing jump input more expressively.

44.q: How is variable jump height usually implemented?
opts: By adding extra gravity while the button is released and the character is still rising
44.why: Extra gravity on release cuts the rise short. Done — the jump height now depends on how long the button is held.
44.wrongWhy: The other answers are different mechanics. The implementation is a gravity change on release, not a new input or state.

44.q: What is the most important quality of a fight?
opts: Readability — the player can answer where the enemy is, what it will do, and what to do about it
44.why: A fight is won or lost on readability. Damage numbers are secondary to whether the player can read the situation.
44.wrongWhy: The other answers are numbers or volume. Readability determines whether the fight is fair.

44.q: What is a telegraph?
opts: A visible wind-up before an enemy attacks
44.why: The wind-up IS the information. The player cannot dodge what they cannot see coming.
44.wrongWhy: The other answers are not telegraphs. A sound alone is weaker; a visible wind-up is the standard.

44.q: Why are instant, untelegraphed attacks a mistake?
opts: The player cannot dodge what they cannot see coming, so the fight becomes memorisation
44.why: Without information the fight is a memory test rather than a skill test. Telegraphs convert it into a fair fight.
44.wrongWhy: The other answers are presentation or performance. The problem is fairness, not appearance.

44.q: What do hitbox and hurtbox mean?
opts: The attacker's damage area and the defender's vulnerable area
44.why: The attacker has a hitbox; the defender has a hurtbox. Keeping the hurtbox smaller than the sprite makes the game feel forgiving.
44.wrongWhy: The other answers are unrelated. The two boxes are the collision areas, not the visuals or the UI.

44.q: What happens without invincibility frames?
opts: A single enemy attack can hit multiple times in one swing and drain a full health bar
44.why: Without i-frames one swing can apply damage every frame it overlaps, which drains the whole bar instantly.
44.wrongWhy: The other answers are unrelated. I-frames exist specifically to prevent multi-hit damage.

44.q: What is the best way to make a crowd feel busy?
opts: Density and variety — many simple characters at different speeds
44.why: A crowd is many simple characters with different speeds. The illusion comes from density, not intelligence.
44.wrongWhy: The other answers are expensive or unrelated. Density and variety create the illusion cheaply.

44.q: What is the cheapest worldbuilding in games?
opts: An ambient character with one sprite, two waypoints, and one line
44.why: A villager walking between two points makes a world feel inhabited. The player's brain fills in the rest.
44.wrongWhy: The other answers are expensive content. Ambient life costs almost nothing and changes how the game feels.

44.q: What makes an NPC memorable?
opts: One rule or quirk, consistently applied
44.why: Players remember NPCs with one quirk far longer than NPCs with complex behaviour.
44.wrongWhy: The other answers add cost without memorability. One quirk is enough.

44.q: Why keep crowds away from the critical path?
opts: Crowds that block the route turn atmosphere into frustration
44.why: Ambient characters should never be required for progression, and they must not be able to block it.
44.wrongWhy: The other answers are not the reason. The problem is gameplay blocking, not cost or appearance.

44.q: What is the layering principle for density?
opts: A few characters close and interactive, many far away and decorative
44.why: Near characters interact; far characters decorate. The far ones can be cheaper because the player looks at them less.
44.wrongWhy: The other answers waste budget. Cheap far characters plus a few detailed near ones is the efficient split.

44.q: What is the failure mode of a progression system?
opts: A long gap with nothing, where the player quits
44.why: Players do not quit at hard parts — they quit at empty parts. The gap is the problem.
44.wrongWhy: The other answers are excess, not failure. Too many rewards is a balance issue, not a retention failure.

44.q: Why should an upgrade change how the player plays?
opts: A bigger number changes nothing; a new route or option changes decisions
44.why: A jump that goes further changes your routes. A bigger damage number changes nothing about how the game plays.
44.wrongWhy: The other answers are not the reason. The value is in changing decisions, not in bigger numbers.

44.q: What is the minimum for a real economy?
opts: Two competing uses for the same resource
44.why: With one use there is no economy, only a queue. Two competing uses force a real trade-off.
44.wrongWhy: The other answers are presentation or volume. Without a trade-off there is no decision.

44.q: What is the purpose of a boss's phase change?
opts: Both escalation and a breather for the player
44.why: Phases give visible progress, escalate the pressure, and provide a natural release between phases.
44.wrongWhy: The other answers are not the purpose. A phase change is a pacing and fairness tool.

44.q: What should a boss's final blow do?
opts: Feel different, with a distinct animation and a moment of safety
44.why: The player should be able to tell they won without the health bar. A boss that dies like a normal enemy wastes the fight.
44.wrongWhy: The other answers are not the purpose. The final blow is the payoff for the whole fight.

44.q: What is the design brief for a boss fight?
opts: A test of everything the player has learned
44.why: A boss that teaches is a tutorial; a boss that surprises is a wall. Familiar mechanics under new pressure is the sweet spot.
44.wrongWhy: The other answers make the boss arbitrary rather than a test.

44.q: What does 'depth' mean in this course?
opts: Combinations of simple systems creating new encounters without new assets
44.why: A fast enemy plus a ranged enemy in the same room is a new encounter without a new asset.
44.wrongWhy: The other answers add volume or complexity. Depth is combinations, not quantity.

44.q: What is the state machine's main benefit?
opts: Visibility: you can see every state and every transition in one place
44.why: Bugs live in the transitions you forgot. A state machine puts all of them in front of you.
44.wrongWhy: The other answers are not the benefit. The value is seeing the whole behaviour at a glance.

44.q: What causes most state-machine bugs?
opts: A state with no exit, or an undefined transition
44.why: If you can get into a state you must be able to get out. Missing rules cause soft-locks.
44.wrongWhy: The other answers are not the source. Missing transitions are the usual cause.

44.q: What is the highest impact-to-effort juice technique?
44.why: A tiny camera offset on impact reads as weight. It is cheap to add and immediately noticeable.
44.wrongWhy: The other answers are expensive for the effect they give. Shake gives the most feel per line of code.

44.q: What does hitstop communicate?
opts: Force and impact — a brief freeze reads as weight
44.why: A 60-80 millisecond freeze on a heavy hit reads as force even though the rules never changed.
44.wrongWhy: The other answers are not what the freeze communicates. It is about impact, not speed or damage.

44.q: Why layer two sounds onto one event?
opts: The combination reads as heavier than either sound alone
44.why: A low thud plus a high crack reads as one heavy impact. Layering is a cheap way to add weight.
44.wrongWhy: The other answers are not the reason. Layering creates a richer single impression.

44.q: Why vary the pitch of a repeated sound?
opts: A sound that repeats identically gets tuned out by the player's brain
44.why: Every repeated sound must vary slightly or the player stops hearing it. A few percent of random variation is enough.
44.wrongWhy: The other answers are not the reason. The problem is the brain filtering out identical repeats.

44.q: What is silence used for in sound design?
opts: A moment of silence after a big event makes the following sound land harder
44.why: Silence is a tool. Removing all sound briefly after a big event increases the impact of the next one.
44.wrongWhy: The other answers misunderstand the purpose. Silence is deliberate, not an absence.

44.q: What is parallax?
opts: Moving background layers at different speeds to create depth
44.why: Parallax is the cheapest depth in games: different speeds per layer read as three-dimensional space.
44.wrongWhy: The other answers are different techniques. Parallax is specifically about layer speeds.

44.q: What does a vignette communicate?
opts: Low health or tension — darkening the screen edges
44.why: Darkening the edges when the player is low on health adds free tension without any new art.
44.wrongWhy: The other answers are not what the vignette signals. It is a state indicator, not an environment effect.

44.q: What is 'camera lead'?
opts: Moving the camera ahead of the player
Moving the camera slightly in the direction the player is moving so they can see what is coming
44.why: Leading the camera lets the player see what is coming in the direction they are moving. It is a one-line change.
44.wrongWhy: The other answers describe other camera behaviours. Lead is specifically about looking ahead.

44.q: What is the principle behind 'squash and stretch'?
opts: Volume stays roughly constant, so squashing wide also squashes short
44.why: When you squash wide you also squash short, and vice versa. Keeping volume constant reads as weight.
44.wrongWhy: The other answers are not the principle. Random scaling or one-directional stretching looks wrong.

44.q: Why animate a state change rather than the object?
opts: A door that tweens open communicates more than a door with a twelve-frame animation
44.why: Animating the transition communicates the change. The player reads the state, not the artwork.
44.wrongWhy: The other answers are not the reason. The communication value is the point.

44.q: What is the test for whether an ambient character is well designed?
opts: It has one rule and a route, and never blocks progression
44.why: Ambient characters cost one sprite and two waypoints. If they can block the player's route, they are a bug, not a world.
44.wrongWhy: The other answers add cost. The test is simplicity plus not interfering with play.

44.q: What is the three-state pattern for an enemy?
44.why: Three states with a visible telegraph on each create readable depth without new art.
44.wrongWhy: The other answers lack the telegraph. The telegraph is what makes the third state fair.

44.q: Why is a fast enemy plus a ranged enemy a new encounter?
opts: The combination creates pressure neither creates alone, without needing new art
44.why: Combinations create depth. The player faces a new problem using assets you already have.
44.wrongWhy: The other answers are not the reason. Depth comes from the combination, not from more content.

44.q: What is the rule about what to cut first?
opts: Extra enemy types, dialogue, save systems, and side content
44.why: Cut extras first. Never cut the core loop, the menu, or the game-over screen.
44.wrongWhy: The other answers list things that must never be cut. They are the minimum viable game.

44.q: What is the test for whether a feature can be cut?
opts: Does removing it change what the player does? If not, it can go
44.why: A second enemy type that behaves identically is not content. If removal changes nothing, it was never a feature.
44.wrongWhy: The other answers are not the test. Cost and difficulty are not the same as lack of impact.

44.q: What is the iteration loop?
opts: Build a tiny thing, play it, change it, play it again
44.why: Short cycles with immediate playtesting surface problems early. Playing is the feedback.
44.wrongWhy: The other answers are longer cycles or skip the playing step. The loop only works if you play each pass.

44.q: How many goals should one iteration pass have?
44.why: One goal per pass, such as 'make the jump feel better'. 'Improve the game' is not a pass.
44.wrongWhy: The other answers make the pass unmeasurable. A single goal lets you know whether it worked.

44.q: What does 'playable beats planned' mean?
opts: A rough playable build every week teaches more than a perfect design document
Play the game instead of making it
44.why: A game you have not played in a month has problems you cannot see, and they compound.
44.wrongWhy: The other answers misunderstand. Planning still happens, but the playable build is the source of truth.

44.q: What is the most important habit in this course?
44.why: One finished game teaches more than five abandoned ones, because finishing includes the parts tutorials skip.
44.wrongWhy: The other answers are not the habit. Finishing is the skill that makes all the others usable.

44.q: Why is the export build important to test?
opts: Missing assets, broken paths, and audio that only works in the editor appear exclusively in the export
44.why: The export is what the player gets. Problems that do not reproduce in the editor will reproduce for players.
44.wrongWhy: The other answers are not the reason. The export is the real product, not the editor view.

44.q: What is the three-state pattern for a player character, in the standard order?
opts: Idle, run, jump, attack, hurt, dead
Run, idle, jump, dead, hurt, attack
Dead, hurt, attack, jump, run, idle
44.why: The standard set is idle, run, jump, attack, hurt, dead. Most forgotten transition: hurt must always return to idle.
44.wrongWhy: The other answers are arbitrary orders. The states matter less than having every exit defined.

44.q: What is the cheapest way to add depth to a fight?
opts: Change the encounter — combine two existing enemy types
44.why: Design the encounter, not the monster. Combinations are free; new art is not.
44.wrongWhy: The other answers change numbers or add cost. The encounter design is the cheap lever.

44.q: What should you do when a bug appears in a state machine?
opts: Add the missing transition to the table first
44.why: Most state bugs are missing rules, not broken code. Find the missing transition before touching the logic.
44.wrongWhy: The other answers patch symptoms. Adding an if adds complexity without fixing the missing rule.

44.q: What is the purpose of the three-state pattern?
opts: To create readable depth without new assets
44.why: Three states with visible telegraphs create depth from behaviour, which costs nothing in art.
44.wrongWhy: The other options change numbers or add art. The pattern's value is behavioural depth.

51.q: What is the actual bar for game art?
51.why: Players judge consistency and readability, not complexity. Clean limited-palette art beats messy detailed art.
51.wrongWhy: The other answers are about quality or quantity. The bar is whether the choices look deliberate.

51.q: How do you improve a silhouette?
opts: Exaggerate — bigger hat, wider shoulders, longer weapon
51.why: Exaggerated shapes read better at small sizes. Detail is the first thing to go when the sprite is small.
51.wrongWhy: The other answers add cost or clutter. Exaggeration is what survives at game size.

51.q: What is the recommended maximum number of colours for a beginner's palette?
opts: Three: background, main, and one accent
51.why: Background, main, one accent. The accent is reserved for things the player must notice.
51.wrongWhy: The other answers either remove contrast or destroy it. Three is the rule that makes the accent work.

51.q: Why must the accent colour be limited?
opts: When everything is accent-coloured, nothing is
51.why: The accent marks what matters. If it is used everywhere it marks nothing.
51.wrongWhy: The other answers are not the reason. The accent works by scarcity.

51.q: Why start pixel art at 16x16?
opts: Small canvases are forgiving — every decision is visible and nothing can hide
51.why: At 16x16 a character is maybe twelve pixels. Nothing can hide, so mistakes are obvious and fixable.
51.wrongWhy: The other answers are not the reason. Small size is a learning tool, not a style choice.

51.q: What is the correct order for drawing a pixel art character?
51.why: Block the silhouette in the main colour, carve with one shade darker and one lighter, add the accent last.
51.wrongWhy: The other answers put detail before structure. The silhouette must be right before any shading is worth doing.

51.q: What is the shading rule that always works?
opts: Light comes from above, so the top edge is lighter and the bottom edge darker
51.why: You do not need to think about lighting — just follow the rule. Top lighter, bottom darker.
51.wrongWhy: The other answers are not the rule. The top-lit convention is what makes shading read correctly.

51.q: Why does two frames at 6 fps beat six frames at 2 fps?
opts: Frame timing matters more than frame count for readability
51.why: Two frames at 6 fps reads as walking; six frames at 2 fps reads as a broken record. Timing carries the motion.
51.wrongWhy: The other answers are technical. The reason is readability of the motion.

51.q: Why should you test animation at the game's actual size?
opts: Animation that looks good zoomed in often looks broken at game size
51.why: Zoom out constantly while drawing. A walk cycle that only works large is not finished.
51.wrongWhy: The other answers are not the reason. Small-size readability is the real test.

51.q: What are Inkscape's three essential operations?
51.why: Union merges shapes, difference cuts one out of another, intersection keeps only the overlap. With those three you can build any icon.
51.wrongWhy: The other answers are basic editing tools. The boolean operations are what make vector art construction possible.

51.q: Why is vector art suited to non-artists?
opts: It is built from primitives and combined shapes, not freehand drawing
51.why: You never draw a line freehand — you move points until a shape looks right. It is construction, not drawing.
51.wrongWhy: The other answers are not the reason. The construction approach is what removes the drawing skill requirement.

51.q: Which asset library is CC0 and commercially safe with no attribution?
51.why: Kenney.nl assets are public domain (CC0): no attribution required, commercial use allowed, no risk.
51.wrongWhy: The other answers host mixed licences. OpenGameArt and itch.io files each carry their own licence and must be checked.

51.q: What must you do before using any asset?
opts: Read the licence — 'free' and 'free to use in your game' are not the same
51.why: Every asset has its own licence. CC0 and CC-BY are safe; CC-BY-SA has share-alike obligations; NC forbids commercial use.
51.wrongWhy: The other answers are workflow steps. The licence determines whether you may use it at all.

51.q: Why keep an asset-credit file from day one?
opts: Retroactive credit hunting is miserable — record source and licence as you go
51.why: When someone asks about an asset, you need the answer immediately. Finding licences after the fact is painful.
51.wrongWhy: The other answers are not the main reason. The file exists because you will need it and cannot reconstruct it later.

51.q: Why should you not mix asset packs from different authors?
opts: Mixed styles look bad; pick one style and stay with it
51.why: Consistency comes from using one style. A game with mismatched packs looks broken even if each asset is good.
51.wrongWhy: The other answers are not the reason. Visual consistency is the goal.

51.q: How do you get character art without drawing or modelling?
opts: Render a 3D model into a flat 2D sprite using an orthographic camera
51.why: Blender renders any model into clean, consistent sprites. Same source means consistent style for free.
51.wrongWhy: The other answers are not practical for a beginner. Rendering avoids both drawing and modelling skill.

51.q: What is the advantage of code-drawn visuals?
opts: They scale perfectly — a code-drawn bar looks identical at every resolution
51.why: An image-based health bar must be redrawn for each resolution; a code-drawn one does not.
51.wrongWhy: The other answers are not the advantage. Resolution independence is the specific benefit.

51.q: What is the foundation of most generated textures?
opts: Noise — a grid of random values smoothed together
51.why: Noise gives clouds, marble, terrain, and rust. Threshold it and you have a texture; tile it and you have a level.
51.wrongWhy: The other answers are not the foundation. Noise plus a threshold is the standard technique.

51.q: Why is a tweened health bar better than one that snaps?
opts: The tween reads as damage; a snap reads as nothing
51.why: The animation communicates the state change. The player reads the transition, not just the value.
51.wrongWhy: The other answers are not the reason. The communication value is the point.

51.q: What is the volume rule in squash and stretch?
opts: Volume stays roughly constant, so squashing wide also squashes short
51.why: Keeping volume constant reads as weight. One-directional stretching looks wrong.
51.wrongWhy: The other answers are incomplete. The constant-volume rule is what makes the effect convincing.

51.q: What is the principle behind 'motion that implies intent'?
opts: Any motion that implies intent reads as animation; the player's brain completes the rest
51.why: A circle that wobbles while moving reads as walking. The player's brain fills in the animation.
51.wrongWhy: The other answers are not the principle. The implication of intent is what creates the illusion.

51.q: What are the four mechanical UI rules?
51.why: Alignment, spacing, hierarchy, contrast. All four are mechanical — you can follow them without design sense.
51.wrongWhy: The other answers are not the rules. These four are the ones that make UI look designed.

51.q: Why is hierarchy important in UI?
opts: If everything is equally prominent, nothing is
51.why: The most important thing must be the biggest or brightest. Equal prominence means no guidance.
51.wrongWhy: The other answers are not the reason. Hierarchy is about directing attention.

51.q: What is the rule about text contrast?
opts: Use light text on light backgrounds
Text must be readable at a glance — if you squint and cannot read it, it fails
Use the smallest font that fits
51.why: Readability is the requirement. Contrast must survive a glance, not a careful look.
51.wrongWhy: The other answers either break readability or are not rules. Glance-readability is the standard.

51.q: How do you get sound effects without making any?
opts: Synthesis tools like sfxr generate effects from sliders
51.why: You do not need sound design knowledge to get a usable jump sound. Sliders plus a randomise button is enough.
51.wrongWhy: The other answers are impractical or illegal. Synthesis is the accessible route.

51.q: What matters more than the quality of a sound?
opts: That every event the player cares about has a sound, and that repeated sounds vary in pitch
51.why: A badly chosen sound beats silence because it confirms the event happened. Variation prevents the brain tuning it out.
51.wrongWhy: The other answers are technical. Presence and variation are what matter perceptually.

51.q: What is the first step in building a level?
opts: Write the level as one sentence of beats, then build only those
51.why: Enter, cross the gap, fight on the platform, climb to the exit. Then build only those beats with placeholder tiles.
51.wrongWhy: The other answers start too late. The beats must exist before any tile is placed.

51.q: Why build a level from placeholder tiles first?
opts: If the layout is not fun with grey boxes, no amount of art will fix it
51.why: Art on an unfun level is wasted art. Playability is a layout property, not an art property.
51.wrongWhy: The other answers are not the reason. The layout must be proven before it is decorated.

51.q: What is the readability rule for walkable versus solid tiles?
opts: They must be distinguishable at a glance
They should be the same colour
51.why: If the player cannot tell where they can walk, the level has failed before it began.
51.wrongWhy: The other answers either remove the distinction or reverse it. Distinguishability is the requirement.

51.q: What is the 30-minute asset workflow's first step?
opts: Decide the silhouette and block it out in one colour
51.why: Minutes 0-5 are silhouette only. No detail until the shape is right.
51.wrongWhy: The other answers come later. Detail before a correct silhouette is wasted work.

51.q: What is the most common trap in the first five minutes?
opts: Perfectionism — refining a silhouette that will be replaced
51.why: Block the shape first; detail comes last. Refining early is wasted effort.
51.wrongWhy: The other answers are later problems. The early trap is spending detail budget on a shape that is still wrong.

51.q: Why decide the final sprite size before you start?
opts: A sprite drawn at 64x64 but displayed at 32x32 loses half its detail
51.why: Drawing at the wrong scale wastes half the work. Decide the display size first.
51.wrongWhy: The other answers are not the reason. Scale mismatch is what wastes the detail.

51.q: What is the secret to a consistent art set?
opts: Same palette, same shading rule, same canvas size for everything
51.why: Consistency comes from process, not talent. Same process plus same palette equals an art style.
51.wrongWhy: The other answers are not the secret. Process consistency is what produces a matching set.

51.q: How many things made with the same process create an art style?
51.why: Make five things the same way and you have an art style. That is the entire secret.
51.wrongWhy: The other answers are wrong quantities. Five is enough to establish a repeatable process.

51.q: What is the purpose of the 30-minute time limit?
opts: It forces decisions — the limit is the point
51.why: A hard time limit prevents perfectionism and forces you to ship something. The constraint is the teaching tool.
51.wrongWhy: The other answers misunderstand. The limit is deliberate, not a shortcut.

51.q: What should you do with a finished but ugly asset?
opts: Keep it — a finished ugly asset teaches more than a perfect unfinished one
51.why: Finishing teaches the process. You now have a workflow you can repeat and improve.
51.wrongWhy: The other answers waste the learning. The value is in completing the loop.

51.q: What does 'steal like an artist' mean in this course?
opts: Study how things work, then apply the principle to your own work
51.why: Reference and study, do not copy. Understanding why something works lets you reproduce the effect legally and originally.
51.wrongWhy: The other answers are literal or counterproductive. The rule is about studying principles, not copying assets.

51.q: What is the rule about using an asset whose licence you cannot find?
opts: Do not use it — there is always another asset
Use it in a prototype only
51.why: If you cannot find the licence, you cannot establish that you may use it. There is always a safe alternative.
51.wrongWhy: The other answers risk infringement. An unknown licence is a forbidden asset.

51.q: What is the 'asset flip' that is banned on most platforms?
51.why: Reselling unmodified assets is both unethical and against most platform rules. Adding your own work is required.
51.wrongWhy: The other answers are normal practice. The banned act is reselling without transformation.

51.q: What is the recommended shading shortcut for pixel art?
opts: Light from above — top lighter, bottom darker
51.why: Follow the convention and you do not have to think about lighting. It always reads correctly.
51.wrongWhy: The other answers either remove depth or are impractical. The convention is the shortcut.

51.q: Why is a limited palette easier than a large one?
opts: Every colour must earn its place, so the important things stand out
51.why: Restraint makes the accent work. With many colours nothing is special.
51.wrongWhy: The other answers are technical. The design benefit is what restraint buys.

51.q: What is the correct order of the five juice techniques by value?
51.why: Shake and hitstop give the most feel for the least work. Start with those two.
51.wrongWhy: The other answers misorder the value. Shake and hitstop are the highest ratio.

51.q: What is the rule about juice and importance?
opts: Juice marks what matters — do not use it everywhere
51.why: If a pickup and a boss death get the same reaction, the player learns nothing is special.
51.wrongWhy: The other answers destroy the signalling function. Juice works by being selective.

51.q: What is the most important thing to test when making a character?
opts: The silhouette — can you tell it apart from the enemy at a glance
51.why: If you cannot tell characters apart from their solid outline, the player cannot read them in motion.
51.wrongWhy: The other answers are secondary. Silhouette readability is the test that matters.

51.q: What is the advantage of rendering 3D models into 2D sprites?
opts: Same source means consistent style for free
51.why: All frames come from one model, so they match automatically. Consistency is free.
51.wrongWhy: The other answers are not the advantage. Consistency from a single source is the benefit.

51.q: What is the recommended way to make a character without drawing?
opts: Design from a verb — 'fast scout' implies a small, forward-leaning silhouette
51.why: Begin with what the character does. The verb implies the silhouette, so you can build it from shapes.
51.wrongWhy: The other answers are not the method. Starting from the verb is what removes the drawing requirement.

51.q: What is the rule about a character's distinctive feature?
51.why: Head, body, one feature. Everything else is noise. The player remembers the one exaggerated thing.
51.wrongWhy: The other answers are not the rule. One exaggerated feature is what survives at small size.

51.q: How do you convey mood without a detailed face?
opts: Posture — a forward lean reads as determined, a hunch reads as tired
51.why: Posture communicates more than facial features. The body alone carries the mood.
51.wrongWhy: The other answers are not the technique. Posture is what reads at a glance.

51.q: What should a character's backstory do?
opts: Justify the design decisions, not decorate them
51.why: One sentence that explains the silhouette. If it does not, the design and the story are fighting.
51.wrongWhy: The other answers misunderstand the purpose. Backstory is a design tool, not content.

51.q: What is the rule about designing a character for its display size?
opts: A character seen at 32 pixels cannot have a detailed face — so do not draw one
51.why: Design for the size the player actually sees. Detail that vanishes at game size is wasted.
51.wrongWhy: The other answers are not the rule. Designing for display size prevents wasted detail.

60.q: What is the difference between CharacterBody2D, StaticBody2D, and Area2D?
opts: CharacterBody2D moves and blocks; StaticBody2D never moves but blocks; Area2D detects without blocking
Area2D moves; the others do not
60.why: Choosing correctly among these three is 90% of getting physics right. Area2D is a sensor — it detects but never blocks.
60.wrongWhy: The other answers either collapse the distinction or reverse it. The blocking behaviour is the whole point.

60.q: What is the difference between is_action_pressed and is_action_just_pressed?
opts: is_action_pressed is true while held; is_action_just_pressed is true only on the frame it was pressed
pressed only works with a keyboard
60.why: Use is_action_pressed for continuous things like running, and is_action_just_pressed for one-shot things like jumping.
60.wrongWhy: The other answers misunderstand the distinction. The frame-level difference is what matters for jumps.

60.q: Why are signals better than direct references?
opts: They keep code decoupled — the player does not need to hold a reference to the health bar
60.why: Decoupled code is easier to change. If the health bar is rebuilt, nothing that emits the signal needs to change.
60.wrongWhy: The other answers are not the reason. Decoupling is the architectural benefit.

60.q: What is the difference between free() and queue_free()?
opts: queue_free() waits until the end of the frame, which is safer than free()
60.why: queue_free() defers deletion to a safe point. Using free() during a signal callback can crash the game.
60.wrongWhy: The other answers are wrong. The safety of deferring deletion is the reason.

60.q: What is the difference between TileMapLayer and TileSet?
opts: TileSet is the collection of tiles and their data; TileMapLayer is the grid that places them
60.why: The TileSet defines what a tile is; the TileMapLayer is where you paint them. Confusing them is a very common beginner error.
60.wrongWhy: The other answers collapse or misstate the distinction.

60.q: What is a state machine's benefit?
opts: It replaces a tangle of if-statements with a list of states and the rules between them
60.why: A state machine makes every state and transition visible in one place. Bugs live in the transitions you forgot.
60.wrongWhy: The other answers are not the benefit. Visibility is the architectural value.

60.q: What is the safest way to store a player's progress?
opts: In a save file under user://, loaded on start
60.why: Progress must persist between runs, so it goes in a file under user://. Variables reset when the game closes.
60.wrongWhy: The other answers do not persist. Only a file under user:// survives closing the game.

60.q: Why does the course recommend testing the exported build?
opts: Missing assets, broken paths, and audio that only works in the editor appear exclusively in the export
60.why: The export is what the player gets. Problems invisible in the editor will be visible to every player.
60.wrongWhy: The other answers are not the reason. The export is the real product.

60.q: What three parts does a good core loop have?
60.why: Kill the enemy (goal), it shoots back (obstacle), it drops coins (reward).
60.wrongWhy: The other lists are structure or screens, not the functional parts of a loop.

60.q: What makes a reward actually a reward?
opts: It changes what the player does next
60.why: If the reward does not change the next loop, it is a score. A real reward alters the player's options.
60.wrongWhy: The other answers are presentation or rarity, which do not change behaviour.

60.q: What is the most common core-loop mistake?
opts: A loop fun for thirty seconds that then repeats identically forever
60.why: The fix is not more content but making the reward change the next loop.
60.wrongWhy: The other answers are not the core problem.

60.q: Which juice technique gives the most feel for the least effort?
60.why: A tiny camera offset on impact reads as weight. Highest impact-to-effort ratio in games.
60.wrongWhy: The other options are expensive visual work with little feel benefit.

60.q: What are the two engines that keep players playing?
60.why: Mastery: I am getting better and can feel it. Curiosity: I want to know what happens next.
60.wrongWhy: The other answers are features or content, not psychological drivers.

60.q: What is the real difficulty dial in most platformers?
60.why: How far back the player restarts determines felt difficulty. It costs progress, not dignity.
60.wrongWhy: The other options change challenge but not felt difficulty as directly.

60.q: What is the three-beat teaching pattern?
60.why: Safe introduction (nothing can go wrong), test (must use it to proceed), twist (combines with something known).
60.wrongWhy: The other patterns miss the essential test beat.

60.q: Why do games have quiet rooms between fights?
opts: They are the release that makes tension meaningful
60.why: Tension needs release. Without the quiet, the fight stops feeling intense.
60.wrongWhy: The other answers misunderstand pacing.

60.q: What is the rule about actions and reactions?
opts: Every action must have a visible reaction, even a failed one
60.why: If the player cannot tell 'it worked' from 'it did nothing', the game has lied.
60.wrongWhy: The other answers allow silent failures, which is the problem the rule prevents.

60.q: What are the three rules of a good death?
opts: Readable, caused by choice, fast to restart
60.why: The player should see what killed them, understand it was their decision, and restart quickly.
60.wrongWhy: The other answers hide the cause or make the player wait.

60.q: What does variable jump height do?
opts: Lets a tap give a small hop and a hold give a full jump
60.why: Button hold time controls height. This single change makes platforming dramatically more controllable.
60.wrongWhy: The other answers add abilities rather than expressive use of the existing input.

60.q: What is the cheapest way to make an enemy more interesting?
opts: Give it three states: idle, telegraph, attack
60.why: Three states with visible telegraphs create depth without new art.
60.wrongWhy: The other answers change numbers or add art.

60.q: What is the cheapest worldbuilding in games?
opts: An ambient character with one sprite, two waypoints, and one line
60.why: A villager walking between two points makes a world feel inhabited. The player's brain fills in the rest.
60.wrongWhy: The other answers are expensive content.

60.q: What is the layering principle for density?
opts: A few close and interactive, many far and decorative
60.why: Near characters interact; far characters decorate. The far ones can be cheaper.
60.wrongWhy: The other answers waste budget.

60.q: What is the failure mode of a progression system?
opts: A long gap with nothing, where the player quits
60.why: Players quit in the gaps, not at the hard parts.
60.wrongWhy: The other answers are excess, not failure.

60.q: What is a boss fight's design brief?
opts: A test of everything the player has learned
60.why: Familiar mechanics under new pressure. A boss that teaches is a tutorial; one that surprises is a wall.
60.wrongWhy: The other answers make the boss arbitrary.

60.q: What does a boss phase change provide?
opts: Both escalation and a breather for the player
60.why: Phases give visible progress, escalate, and provide a natural release between phases.
60.wrongWhy: The other answers are incomplete or not the purpose.

60.q: What is the highest impact-to-effort juice technique?
60.why: A tiny camera offset reads as weight. Most feel per line of code.
60.wrongWhy: The other answers are expensive for the effect.

60.q: Why animate a state change rather than the object?
opts: A door that tweens open communicates more than one with a twelve-frame animation
60.why: Animating the transition communicates the change. The player reads the state, not the artwork.
60.wrongWhy: The other answers are not the reason.

60.q: What is the most important habit in the whole course?
60.why: One finished game teaches more than five abandoned ones, because finishing includes what tutorials skip.

60.q: What is the purpose of a shipping checklist?
opts: The last ten percent is a checklist, not a skill — future you will be tired and forget things
60.why: Menu, pause, restart, game over, export, icon, credits. None of it is glamorous and all of it is required.
60.wrongWhy: The other answers are not the purpose.

60.q: What is the fastest way to improve as a developer?
opts: Enter a game jam — a deadline forces you to finish
60.why: A deadline is the fastest teacher available. Jams force finishing and originality.
60.wrongWhy: The other answers are slower or avoid the finishing skill.

60.q: What is the final thing this course asks you to do?
